description: A tool that checks whether a difference between two space images is real or just a change of colour.
summary:
TIMEFRAME/102 asks whether a source in SPHEREx data is moving, changing in brightness, or just seen at a different colour. Every SPHEREx exposure has its own date and wavelength, so a change in flux can come from either.

I built a Python pipeline that measures one control star in 80 SPHEREx cutouts from IRSA, applies a written quality policy, and writes one validated case file. A single-page viewer shows each frame's date and wavelength side by side, with a blink comparator, a spectral plot, and a table of all 80 observations. Excluded frames stay listed with reasons.

The result is honest: 61 frames were usable, and the verdict is "insufficient evidence" for both motion and variability. I could not measure a systematic floor, because no frame had the 20 comparison stars I required in advance, so I claim neither variability nor constancy.

This matters because a null result that states exactly why it is null, with its limits visible, is a safer base for finding real moving or changing sources than a confident claim. Code, viewer and slides were written with AI assistance.
details:
TIMEFRAME/102 asks whether a source in SPHEREx data is moving, changing in brightness, or simply seen at a different colour. Every SPHEREx exposure has its own date and its own wavelength, so a change in flux can come from either.

I built a Python pipeline that measures flux and position for one control star (Gaia DR3 1633306316700113024) in 80 planned SPHEREx cutouts from IRSA, applies a written quality policy, and writes one validated case file (schema 1.8.0). I also built a single-page viewer that reads that file and shows the date and wavelength of every frame side by side, with a blink comparator, a spectral plot, a table of all 80 observations (excluded frames stay listed with reasons), provenance, and outlier marks read from the file. A Planet X calculator shows the apparent shift for typed-in distances; it is an educational approximation, not an orbit fit or a detection.

Result: 61 of 80 frames were usable over 52 nights, spanning 0.76 to 4.99 micrometres. My verdict for both motion and spectral variability is "insufficient evidence". I could not measure a systematic photometric floor or an astrometric threshold, because no frame had the 20 vetted comparison stars I required in advance (1 to 7 per frame). So I make no claim of variability or of constancy. I report my limits openly: the outlier screen was written after exploratory inspection, one outlier is unexplained, cutout wavelengths differ from the public calibration map by up to 14.5 nm on some detectors, and my injection test is simulated and tests the code only.

Intended impact: a small, auditable way to keep time and colour separate in SPHEREx data, and a null result that states exactly why it is null.

Tools: Python (libraries listed in the repository), HTML and JavaScript for the viewer, IRSA SPHEREx cutouts, 2MASS and AllWISE catalogues, Gaia DR3, and the VizieR service.

AI use: I wrote the backend code with Codex and the viewer, slides and this text with Claude. I set and checked the analysis rules and conclusions myself. IRSA MOST and JPL Horizons were used only to explore an asteroid case (Victoria): I compared MOST positions with Horizons geocentric positions (median difference about 1.1 arcsec), but the asteroid case was not completed, so neither tool feeds the results above. https://rishavjha8515-hub.github.io/timeframe102/
projectRefs: VizieR (CDS), used as the catalogue fallback
